claim: Pons (2018 AER) achieved precinct-level randomization of door-to-door canvassing in France's 2012 presidential campaign because the five-million-door scale allowed randomization at the administrative vote-recording unit itself, unlike prior individual-level GOTV experiments.
stance_target: bureau-de-vote-level causal evidence exists for targeting canvassing resources in France
scope_conditions: France, 2012 presidential campaign, PS canvassing operation
quoted_support: While existing experiments randomized door-to-door visits at the individual level, the scale of this campaign (five million doors knocked) enabled randomization by precinct, the level at which vote shares are recorded administratively.

claim: Door-to-door canvassing in the 2012 Hollande campaign had no significant effect on voter turnout but increased Hollande's vote share by 3.2 points in round 1 and 2.8 points in round 2, both significant at 5%.
stance_target: canvassing is a persuasion tool, not primarily a mobilization tool
scope_conditions: France, 2012 presidential election, precincts allocated to canvassers vs control
quoted_support: I find that it increased Francois Hollande's vote share in precincts allocated to canvassers by 3.2 and 2.8 percentage points in the first and second rounds of the presidential elections... significant at the 5 percent level.

claim: The persuasion effect of 2012 door-to-door canvassing persisted into subsequent elections: PS candidates gained about 0.66-0.7 points in the 2012 legislative elections and roughly 47% of the original effect size carried through to the 2014 European elections before further decay.
stance_target: canvassing effects are durable enough to matter for multi-cycle targeting strategy, not just the immediate election
scope_conditions: France, precincts canvassed in 2012 tracked through 2012 legislative and 2014 European elections
quoted_support: the impact of the visits almost entirely persisted in these elections by 0.7 percentage points. This effect was larger than the victory margin of members of parliament from the PS elected in 2012 in 5.9 percent of the constituencies. Persistence to the 2014 European elections was smaller (about 47 percent of the original effect).

claim: Statistical tests (SUR framework) reject the hypothesis that canvassing's vote-share effect is fully explained by mobilizing left-wing non-voters, implying persuasion of undecided/swing voters is the dominant mechanism, not turnout mobilization.
stance_target: canvassing works mainly by persuasion of undecided voters, relevant to how militant targeting should be modeled (swing precincts vs. base-mobilization precincts)
scope_conditions: France 2012, SUR comparison of turnout and vote-share treatment effects
quoted_support: I reject (at the 5 or 10 percent level) the null hypothesis that the effects on turnout and vote shares were equal, in all but one specification. These results suggest that the increase in Hollande's vote share was driven by persuasion more than by the mobilization of left-wing non-voters.
numbers: comparison: Gerber & Green (2000) 15.6%, Green et al. (2003) 11.5%

claim: Only 48% of doors knocked in the 2012 campaign were actually opened, and treatment precincts were not fully canvassed, requiring an instrumental-variables (local average treatment effect) design to distinguish intent-to-treat from actual treatment-on-treated.
stance_target: methodological caveat for interpreting canvassing-effect magnitudes
quoted_support: Since 48 percent of the doors knocked by canvassers opened, I scale the point estimates by 1/0.48 and find that 6.7 percent and 5.7 percent of the voters living in households that opened their door were persuaded to vote for François Hollande.

claim: No comprehensive database of French voter/electoral precinct (bureau de vote) boundaries existed as of this study, forcing the author to reconstruct precinct assignment from 2011 voter registers rather than an official crosswalk.
stance_target: bureau-de-vote boundary data / crosswalks are a genuine, longstanding obstacle in France, corroborating axis 2 of the research query on INSEE/data.gouv crosswalk difficulty
quoted_support: There does not exist any comprehensive database of the boundaries of French voter precincts, which are [reconstructed from] registers in all sufficiently large municipalities.

claim: The 2012 Hollande door-to-door campaign cost $29 million, 38 times less than Barack Obama's 2012 US campaign budget, reflecting canvassing's status as a cost-efficient mobilization channel favored by resource-constrained French campaigns.
stance_target: cost-effectiveness rationale for door-to-door as the dominant French field tactic
quoted_support: François Hollande's 2012 campaign spent 29 million dollars, 38 times less than Barack Obama's.
